name: Sun Yellow
lede: Sun yellow is a bright, warm yellow-orange named for the sun; it has also been a pigment synonym for a nickel titanium yellow and a dictionary word for maize.

sections.title: Three uses of one name
sections.body:
As a plain color word, sun yellow is a bright yellow; Paterson sends the reader to *maize* [1]. Maize in turn is sometimes a bright yellow and also a pale yellow used for dress fabric, and Paterson says sun yellow is another name for it [1]. The swatch here is deeper and more orange than the word suggests, close to [[golden-yellow]] and [[mustard]] territory.

In the paint trade it meant something else. The pigment literature gives sun yellow as a synonym for a nickel titanium yellow, also called titan yellow, in Colour Index number 77788 [2]. That is a modern industrial pigment [2]. Related pages: [[maize]] and [[yellow]].

sections.title: Is the sun yellow?
sections.body: The name leans on a habit of seeing. Paterson points out that from space the sun appears white, and that it looks yellow from earth because the atmosphere filters the blue end of sunlight [1]. Birren's survey of color theory quotes Aristotle, who gave fire and the sun the color yellow [3]. Pastoureau quotes the French lexicographer Furetière, who wrote that yellow reflects the most light after white, which is why painters paint the sun's rays yellow [4]. It is a convention, a good one, but not a measurement.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Sun yellow appears in 0.3% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive, 71 paintings, as photographed, more common than 58% of the named colors [5]. It almost always plays an accent: 95% of the 92 paintings where we measure roles [5]. It peaks in the 1800s, at 0.7% of 8,345 paintings, 1.7x the baseline of the same museums [5].

George Dawe has it in 9 of 50 works here, 10.4x his museums' baseline, and the United Kingdom is the most over-represented country at 4.6x [5]. The earliest match, 1375, is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, 552 years before the name's earliest record in our sources, the 1927 RAL list [5].
